newsitem.title: FRANCE: POLL - French deficit overshoot seen in 1997, 1998.
newsitem.headline: POLL - French deficit overshoot seen in 1997, 1998.

text.p: France's budget deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product is expected to overshoot the three percent target for joining a European single currency in both 1997 and 1998, a Reuter poll of 23 economists published on Wednesday showed.
The deficit was seen at 3.3 percent of GDP this year and at 3.1 percent next year, while the economy was seen expanding by 2.2 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
The poll was conducted between July 9 and 16, before the results of an audit of public finances were released and before new tax measures aimed at reducing the deficit were unveiled on Monday.

Some economists said they were now slightly more optimistic about the prospects for the French deficit following the introduction of the new measures and that the chances of hitting three percent next year were higher.
Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch, said, "3.3 is likely for this year and there is so much flexibility in these accounts it's possible we could see 3.0 percent next year."

In the previous Reuter poll published in April the consensus for the 1997 deficit was 3.0 percent. However economists revised their predictions after the election of the new Socialist government said public finances were worse than previously thought and that it would not try and hit 3.0 percent in 1997 come what may.

"The reality was 3.6 percent after the election as there was no commitment to rein in the state deficit," Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, said. "Now the decisions have been taken we're back to square one...but with higher taxes."
The poll also showed that few economists expected the new Socialist government's pledge to reduce unemployment to have a major impact in the next two years.

The median forecast for the 1997 unemployment rate was 12.5 percent, unchanged from the rate in May, coming down to 12.3 percent in 1998. The median forecast for the fourth quarter of next year was 12.1 percent.

The decline in the franc against the dollar was seen bottoming out in the third quarter of 1997. The franc was seen climbing back past 6.0 in the fourth quarter of this year and reaching 5.73 per dollar by the end of next year.
The franc fell to 6.1527 against the dollar on Wednesday, its lowest level this year and a slide of 19 percent since the beginning of the year.

Economists said the decline in the franc against the dollar was expected to boost the French trade performance and most had revised their predictions for the current account up since the previous April poll.
However sluggish domestic investment, not helped by weak consumer demand, low inflation and the new corporate tax measures, was seen offsetting the strong export performance.

"The real problem we're seeing this year is that the export sector is compensated by weaker than expected investment," Perez said. "With the change in the corporate position (on Monday) there's no reason to see investment picking up."
Predictions for the franc against the mark showed that most expected European monetary union to go ahead even if the 1997 public deficit were to overshoot the strict three percent target.

According to the median forecast in the survey, the franc was seen hitting 3.35 per mark, close to its central parity of 3.3539, in the second quarter of next year and staying there until the scheduled single currency launch in 1999.

"Once the political decisions have been taken the central banks will be free to do what they want...and they want the central parities. With no more political risks they can have huge intervention in the markets to keep the rates there," Chaney said.
